                            PETITION FOR REVIEW

      Pursuant to Section 313(b) of the Federal Power Act, 16 U.S.C. § 825l(b),

Rule 15(a) of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, and D.C. Circuit Rule 15,

the Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana, Citizens Utility Board of Illinois, and

Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin (collectively “Petitioners”) petition this Court

for review of the following orders issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (“FERC”), as well as any subsequent amendment or modification of

the following orders:




                                          1
     Order on Complaint re Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company v.

      Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Docket No. EL26-38-000,

      194 FERC ¶ 61,214 (Mar. 19, 2026) (the “Order”) (Attachment A).

    Notice of Denial of Rehearing by Operation of Law and Providing for

      Further Consideration, Docket No. EL26-38-001, 195 FERC ¶ 62,110 (May

      21, 2026) (“Rehearing Denial Order”) (Attachment B).

      Both orders were issued under the Federal Power Act and are thus subject to

judicial review under 16 U.S.C. § 825l.

      The Petitioners participated in the proceedings before FERC. Both

Petitioners filed timely motions to intervene on January 26, 2026. On April 20,

2026, Petitioners timely sought rehearing of the Order (Attachment C). FERC has

denied Petitioners’ request for rehearing. See Rehearing Denial Order. Petitioners’

petition is filed within sixty days after the denial of rehearing. 16 U.S.C. § 825l(b).

This Court has subject matter jurisdiction, Petitioners are parties aggrieved by the

Order, and venue is proper. Id. § 825l(a)–(b)

Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.

                                  ORDER ON COMPLAINT

                                   (Issued March 19, 2026)

       On January 5, 2026, Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company (SIGE) filed a
complaint (Complaint) pursuant to sections 202(c), 306, and 309 of the Federal Power
Act (FPA)1 and Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,2
proposing revisions to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO)
Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (Tariff) to add
a provision (Proposed Tariff Provision) to allocate the costs of keeping Unit 2 of the F.B.
Culley generating plant (Culley Unit 2) in operation, in response to the U.S. Department
of Energy’s (DOE) December 23, 2025 Emergency Order No. 202-25-13 (DOE Order),
under section 202(c) of the FPA and section 301 of the DOE Organization Act.3

       In this order, we grant the Complaint and find that the Proposed Tariff Provision is
just and reasonable, subject to the outcome of the proceeding in Docket No. ER25-3425.
We direct MISO to make a compliance filing, within 30 days of the date of a Commission
order accepting MISO’s compliance filing in Docket No. ER25-3425, to adopt the
Proposed Tariff Provision, as revised, as discussed below.

I.     Background

       A.        Culley Unit 2 Retirement Plan

        Culley Unit 2, located in southwestern Indiana, is a coal-fired unit that has a
nameplate capacity of 103.7 MW. Culley Unit 2 is owned and operated by SIGE, a
utility operating subsidiary of CenterPoint Energy, Inc. SIGE planned to retire the unit
on December 31, 2025, pursuant to commitments SIGE made in a settlement agreement
approved by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (Indiana Commission) in 2025.4
SIGE submitted a notice to suspend operation of Culley Unit 2 to MISO pursuant to
Attachment Y of the Tariff, and MISO found no reliability violations.

       B.        DOE Order

        In the DOE Order, the Secretary of Energy determined that “an emergency
exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric
energy, a shortage of facilities for the generation of electric energy, and other causes.”5
Further, the Secretary of Energy determined that issuance of the DOE Order will “meet
the emergency and serve the public interest.”6 Therefore, the Secretary of Energy
directed MISO and SIGE to take all measures necessary to ensure that Culley Unit 2
is available to operate7 and directed SIGE to keep Culley Unit 2 open for 90 days, i.e.,
until March 23, 2026.8

        The DOE Order cited a statement in the 2024 North American Electric Reliability
Corporation (NERC) Long-Term Reliability Assessment (Reliability Assessment) that
MISO is at risk because “probabilistic assessments indicate above-normal generator
outages during extreme weather can result in unserved energy or load loss. With
uncertainty around new resource additions and existing generator retirements, MISO
is also at risk of falling below [Reference Margin Levels] within the next five years.”9
The DOE Order quoted a MISO April 2025 presentation on the Planning Resource

      The DOE Order directed SIGE to “file with [this Commission] Tariff revisions or
waivers [necessary] to effectuate [the DOE Order].”14

       Several entities filed requests for rehearing of the DOE Order with DOE.

II.    SIGE’s Complaint

       SIGE states that it and MISO agree that the Tariff does not have a mechanism
for SIGE to recover costs incurred under the DOE Order. SIGE therefore asks the
Commission to exercise its authority under FPA sections 202(c), 306, and 309 to
order MISO to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision as a cost recovery and allocation
mechanism. SIGE also states that the Proposed Tariff Provision is strictly to establish
a cost allocation mechanism, and that, after the 90-day period (Order Duration Period),
SIGE will submit a filing in a separate docket with the actual costs to be allocated

        SIGE asserts that the Proposed Tariff Provision meets the “just and reasonable”
standard of section 202(c)(1). In support, SIGE states that section 202(c) requires costs
to be allocated based on the scope and nature of the emergency and that the DOE Order
referred to the MISO North and MISO Central regions; accordingly, SIGE argues that
allocating SIGE’s costs of complying with the DOE Order to both the MISO North and
MISO Central regions comports with section 202(c)’s just and reasonable standard.16
SIGE notes that the Proposed Tariff Provision is similar to the Tariff provision approved
by the Commission with regard to the Consumers Energy Company (Consumers) J.H.
Campbell plant (Campbell Plant), and the geographic scope identified in the DOE Order
is virtually identical to the scope identified in the DOE emergency order on the Campbell
Plant (Campbell Plant DOE Order).17

       The Proposed Tariff Provision specifies that it is pursuant to the DOE Order
and applies to the allocation of costs (DOE Order Costs) associated with the continued
availability of Culley Unit 2 pursuant to the DOE Order and any extensions ordered by
the Secretary of Energy. The Proposed Tariff Provision states that SIGE will petition the
Commission to approve recovery of DOE Order Costs, net of market revenues, and that
the costs will be allocated among Local Resource Zones18 1-7, i.e., among zones in the
MISO North and MISO Central regions, to load-serving entities (LSE) on a “load ratio
share” basis. SIGE notes that the issue of cost allocation on a demand or energy basis is

       SIGE argues that the Commission’s prior notice requirements, filed rate
doctrine, and rule against retroactive ratemaking apply to filings or proceedings under
sections 205 and 206 of the FPA, but do not apply to determinations and cost recovery
under section 202(c).20 SIGE argues that section 202(c) allows costs to be determined
and recovered after the emergency generation or provision of jurisdictional service.
SIGE maintains that section 202(c)’s contemplation of such post-hoc determinations and
recovery is demonstrated in the wording of the statute, including that, after an emergency
order “takes effect,” there will be “supplemental” orders regarding “compensation or
reimbursement.”21 Alternatively, SIGE requests that, if the Commission determines that
a section 206 proceeding is necessary, including a finding that the Tariff is unjust and
unreasonable and a subsequent determination as to a just and reasonable rate, then the
Proposed Tariff Provision should be made effective as of the date of filing of the
Complaint.22

       A.        MISO Answer

       MISO agrees with SIGE that the Tariff does not currently contain a mechanism
for cost allocation under these circumstances.25 MISO states that it does not oppose
the Proposed Tariff Provision and that it will file such a schedule if directed by the
Commission. MISO notes that it reserves the right to change the cost allocation
mechanism “to account for existing Tariff requirements and to include other clarifications
as may be appropriate.”26

       B.        Comments and Protests

        The Michigan Attorney General and the Illinois Commission state that, contrary
to claims made by the DOE Order, there is no evidence of an energy emergency.27 The
Illinois Commission asserts that MISO does not need the capacity provided by Culley
Unit 2 and that MISO has emergency operating procedures, which both belie the notion
of an emergency in MISO.28 The Illinois Commission further states that the DOE Order
is an overreach of federal authority because it encroaches on that state’s role in resource
adequacy and fuel choice.29

        The Michigan Attorney General opposes the Proposed Tariff Provision, arguing
that the Commission should reject it because the underlying DOE Order justifying
cost recovery is ultra vires, and, absent a valid legal obligation to operate pursuant
to FPA section 202(c), the imposition of the costs of operating Culley Unit 2 on
ratepayers pursuant to FPA sections 205 or 206 is not just and reasonable and is unduly
discriminatory or preferential, and violates the filed rate doctrine. Alternatively, the
Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission, under the discretion afforded
the Commission under FPA section 202(c), issue an order deferring any finding, on the
basis that the Proposed Tariff Provision is premature until the rehearing requests at DOE
are resolved.30 The Michigan Attorney General also asserts that the Commission should
limit cost recovery to those costs from the limited scope of operation ordered by the DOE

        Public Interest Organizations also argue that the Commission cannot approve any

        Further, Public Interest Organizations explain that MISO has existing Tariff
provisions to compensate for and allocate the costs of Culley Unit 2’s participation in
the energy and ancillary services market, as the Tariff compensates generators during
periods of scarcity through the Value of Lost Load (VOLL) mechanism, which is a
price cap implemented during MISO emergency events.40 Given this Tariff mechanism,
Public Interest Organizations argue that SIGE must demonstrate that recovery of its
costs are not compensated by existing Tariff provisions.41 In addition, Public Interest
Organizations argue that SIGE should demonstrate what, if any, uncompensated benefits
are provided by the continued operation of Culley Unit 2 and the relative level of benefits
each Local Resource Zone receives.42 Public Interest Organizations allege that SIGE has
not justified the load ratio share concept in the Proposed Tariff Provision, as the benefits
of the continued operation of the unit do not appear to align with the average amount of
electricity withdrawn by each LSE.43

       Multiple commenters request that the Commission require MISO to initiate a
stakeholder process related to the Proposed Tariff Provision.44 The Illinois Attorney
General argues that the DOE Order may be extended or other section 202(c) orders may

       OMS asserts that to satisfy the just and reasonable standard required by law,
any cost allocation method must demonstrate a clear nexus between the costs incurred
and the benefits received, and in evaluating whether such a relationship exists, material
differences among states and regions must be considered, including variations in load
forecasts, resource mix, retirement schedules, and system conditions.50 OMS states that
routine Commission approval of broad allocation for costs associated with a section
202(c) order may incentivize utilities to accelerate retirements and cash in on a section
202(c) order cost shift, moving costs away from local customers and onto an 11-state

for the cost allocation method to allocate costs in accordance with the scope of the
emergency as described by the DOE Order. We recognize that the parties offer different
interpretations of the DOE Order on that issue. SIGE argues that the beneficiaries are the
LSEs in Local Resource Zones 1-7, which the DOE Order refers to as MISO North and

DOE Order supports a MISO-wide cost allocation, including to MISO South.68

DOE Order defined the geographic scope of the emergency. However, we find that, as
with the Campbell Plant DOE Order, the most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s
intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued operation of Culley
Unit 2 is in the MISO North and MISO Central regions, i.e., Local Resource Zones 1-7.
